Abstract—This study investigates the thermal performance of
a high-speed Solid Rotor Induction Machine (SRIM) equipped
with a forced air-cooling system. Electromagnetic losses are
first computed using Finite Element Analysis (FEA) in ANSYS
Maxwell, with particular focus on rotor losses in the Fe52
solid rotor material. These losses serve as inputs to a thermal
network model in MotorCAD, enabling a detailed temperature
distribution assessment. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
simulations further evaluate how rotor temperature impacts
overall cooling performance. Results from the combined elec-
tromagnetic–thermal approach highlight the highest temperature
concentrations in the rotor region, emphasizing the importance
of effective cooling design. By demonstrating how forced air-
cooling manages heat dissipation—particularly through radial
ducts—the study shows how proper thermal management can
significantly enhance both the operational efficiency and longevity
of high-speed SRIMs. Future work will explore advanced cooling
materials and optimize cooling geometry to further improve
machine reliability and performance.
I. INTRODUCTION
Electrical machines play a vital role in a wide range of
applications, from home appliances to industrial machinery. In
the context of global sustainability, these machines must meet
various criteria that encompass not only physical and techno-
logical factors but also environmental considerations [1]. One
crucial aspect of their performance is thermal management,
which is essential for ensuring efficiency and longevity. High
temperatures if not properly managed can lead to overheating,
potentially reducing the machine’s lifespan and performance.
In recent years, SRIMs have garnered considerable interest
for applications requiring robustness, reliability, and the ability
to operate in harsh environments, particularly in high-speed
systems critical to various applications such as pumps, gas
turbines, and high-power-density machines.
The history of SRIMs, including prototypes, can be found
from literature, e.g. an axially-slitted solid rotor with 30 kW
power and 24 kr/min speed . The study includes a comparison
of 2-pole and 4-pole SRIM prototypes, verifying by measure-
ments that the 2-pole machine has lower stator core and rotor
losses, but higher temperature rise than the 4-pole machine.
Pyrh¨onen and Nerg et al. contributed to the development of
SRIM with an 8 MW SRIM operating at 12 kr/min, and a
remarkable 10 MW variant specifically tailored for hermetic
natural gas compression applications featuring a copper cage
within the solid rotor core.
SRIMs have a well-documented history in the literature.
For example, [2] describes an axially slitted solid rotor rated
at 30 kW, running at 24 kr/min. That work compares 2-pole
and 4-pole SRIM prototypes, showing that while the 2-pole
machine exhibits lower stator core and rotor losses, it also
experiences a higher temperature rise than the 4-pole machine.
Pyrh¨onen and Nerg et al. [3] introduced an 8 MW SRIM
operating at 12 kr/min and, subsequently, a 10 MW variant
designed for hermetic compression of natural gas. This larger
machine incorporates a copper cage within the solid rotor core
for enhanced performance and Ortiz et al. [ [4]] analyzed
the same machine discussed in this paper, adding a thin
copper coating on the rotor surface and achieving improved
torque across various slip values. Although this copper layer
introduces additional losses, it boosts overall electromagnetic
torque, ultimately paving the way for greater power density
when paired with efficient cooling strategies.
The thermal management of high-speed machines presents
challenges because the components of electrical machines,
including air gap, stator and rotor laminations, windings, wind-
ing insulation, and magnets, have varying thermal properties.
The lumped-parameter thermal networks (LPTNs) were widely
used in the past to estimate the temperature distribution by
dividing the whole machine into discrete thermal ”nodes”
connected by thermal resistances capacitances [5]. These mod-
els provide quick, system-level simulations which are useful
for early design decisions. However, LTPNs utilize simplified


assumptions that less accurate for complex geometries, may
not capture local hot spots especially in high-speed electrical
machines [6].
Therefore, thermal behavior and fluid flow in electrical
machines are usually analyzed with CFD. For example, Liao et
al. [7] examined air flow and heat transfer in high performance
motors using the CFD tool. While Howey et al. [8] discussed
the temperature distribution in rotating machines focusing on
air-gap convection. I
In [9] an optimization algorithm is employed to reduce
computational time in CFD-based thermal modeling of elec-
trical machines. By parameterizing the axial location of a
stator vent, the optimization process minimizes peak stator
temperature and reduces computational and user time. The
results show that the optimal vent position can lower the
peak temperature by 9.4 K. Additionally, a sensitivity study
develops a polynomial relationship between vent position
and peak temperature, while detailed analysis of mass flow
and pressure distribution further informs the cooling design.
This approach highlights the potential of integrating CFD
simulations with optimization algorithms to improve thermal
management in electrical machines.
The aim of this paper is to study the temperature distribution
and internal flow field in a high-speed induction machine with
CFD. The iron losses in the rotor were predicted by the FEA
method and LTPN was used to predict the temperatures using
air forced cooling method to compare with CFD results.

The stator is constructed using non-oriented laminated elec-
trical steel NO20, which minimizes core losses. The rotor is
manufactured from a solid Fe52 iron block, chosen for its
exceptional tensile strength and durability, ensuring reliable
operation within the high-speed range. In this configuration,
the dominant source of losses arises in the rotor from eddy
currents induced at high frequencies, which significantly in-
fluence the rotor losses and torque generation.
III. LOSSES CALCULATION
The electrical loss distribution in a SRIM mainly consists of
core iron losses in the stator and rotor losses, both contributing
significantly to overall energy dissipation. Rotor losses stem
from multiple factors, including mechanical friction, windage
losses, and eddy current losses. This study focuses exclusively
on the last one, which result from induced currents in the
motor’s conductive components.

Joule losses in conductive materials, as expressed in equation

As this study focuses on rotor temperature calculations
using FEA, it is essential to account for the significance
of time-stepping in high-speed machines, as rotational speed
greatly impacts the accuracy of the simulation results. The


precision of time-stepping results is first studied by varying
the time step length, corresponding to a reasonable step of
1 degree of rotation. Since this paper focuses on thermal
analysis, results at a single operating point are sufficient for
comparison with CFD simulation results for this machine,
which are obtained at 2% slip, rotating at 23,520 rpm.
The results of the FEA simulations show average rotor
losses calculated as solid losses of 1086.5W. Fig.1 illustrates
the loss density generated in the rotor, highlighting that the
losses are predominantly concentrated on the rotor surface,
where eddy currents are most pronounced.

IV. THERMAL MODELING
Thermal modeling is essential in electrical machines to
ensure performance and reliability. In solid rotor induction
machines (SRIMs), heat dissipation is challenging due to the
rotor’s solid structure, requiring accurate thermal analysis.
MotorCAD is widely used for thermal modeling, partic-
ularly for simulating cooling methods such as forced air
cooling and radial ducts, which are key features of the machine
analyzed in this study. However, MotorCAD cannot perform
electromagnetic simulations of solid rotor machines, making
it unsuitable for directly determining rotor losses. To address
this, an ANSYS Maxwell 2D model was developed to compute
the losses in the stator, winding, and rotor at 2% slip, which
were then used as inputs in MotorCAD’s thermal network.

The results of the LTPN model in MotorCAD provide a
detailed temperature distribution of the SRIM under forced
air cooling. The LTPN method simplifies heat transfer analysis
by representing the machine’s components as interconnected
thermal resistances and capacitances, allowing for an efficient
estimation of temperature variations over time.

Maxwell were used directly as input for the thermal model in
MotorCAD. The cooling system consists of forced ventilation
through radial ducts, designed with two air inlets and two
outlets, ensuring continuous airflow through the stator, airgap,
and winding regions. The model was simulated with an initial
ambient temperature of 40 ° C and a fluid volume flow rate of
1497 liters/min, representing the cooling airflow. A transient
thermal calculation was performed to analyze the evolution
of the temperature over time. As shown in Fig.2, the results
indicate that the highest temperature concentration occurs in
the rotor, where most of the losses are dissipated, highlighting
the critical role of effective cooling in maintaining thermal
stability.
Fig. 2: SRIM LPTN thermal model results.
V. CFD ANALYSIS
Effective temperature management in electrical machines
is essential for safe operation and extended longevity. CFD
is a proven method to accurately predict the temperature
distribution and fluid flow within these machines [12].
In this study, the geometry of the electrical machine was
initially created using Ansys Maxwell and then exported
to SpaceClaim in Ansys Fluent for model preparation and
cleaning as shown in Fig. 3. The meshing tool in Ansys Fluent
was employed to generate a high-quality mesh in Fig. 4 suited
for CFD simulations. ANSYS Fluent setup was then used
to simulate temperature distribution and fluid flow, aiming to
predict heat transfer characteristics and identify potential hot
spots within the machine.

VI. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
This paper presents the thermal analysis of a high-speed
SRIM using FEA and CFD to evaluate rotor surface tempera-
ture and the cooling system’s effectiveness in transferring heat
from the rotor through the air gap to the exterior. Preliminary
results confirm the model’s accuracy, predicting a rotor surface
temperature of 474 K and a steady pressure drop in the air gap.
Fig. 7 shows an experimental prototype, which currently
available in the laboratory, reflecting the dimensions and
configuration used to analyze the cooling system of the solid
rotor. In the future, the results obtained from testing of this
prototype will be compared with the current simulatioresults.
More detailed analysis will be done to compare with the
experimental results.

Abstract: This study investigates the thermal performance of a high-speed Solid Rotor Induction Machine (SRIM) equipped with a forced air-cooling system. Electromagnetic losses are first computed using Finite Element Analysis (FEA) in ANSYS Maxwell, with particular focus on rotor losses in the Fe52 solid rotor material. These losses serve as inputs to a thermal network model in MotorCAD, enabling a detailed temperature distribution assessment. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations further evaluate how rotor temperature impacts overall cooling performance. Results from the combined elec- tromagnetic–thermal approach highlight the highest temperature concentrations in the rotor region, emphasizing the importance of effective cooling design. By demonstrating how forced air- cooling manages heat dissipation—particularly through radial ducts—the study shows how proper thermal management can significantly enhance both the operational efficiency and longevity of high-speed SRIMs. Future work will explore advanced cooling materials and optimize cooling geometry to further improve machine reliability and performance.
